prize_parts.citation: for showing how borrowing limits tied to collateral values feed back on asset prices, so that shocks are amplified and propagated into persistent credit cycles

statement.case_for: My preferred part is unchanged: a single award to Kiyotaki and Moore for the 1997 collateral-constraint mechanism. I judge it on three criteria. It supplies a new explanatory framework, the framework has had lasting influence, and the credit can be assigned precisely. The loop is simple. Credit limits depend on collateral values, collateral values depend on the credit those limits allow, and so a small shock to net worth becomes large, persistent and spreading. Nearly thirty years of reuse as a building block for financial-friction models and post-2008 policy analysis settles the maturity question. The two-author origin makes the exact credit unusually clean. Round 1 changed one thing. I had proposed Gertler as a third name. Hassler, Krusell, Andersson and Stromberg argued that the accelerator works through borrower net worth and external finance premia. They also argued that it is entangled with the work recognised in 2022 and that it splits Gertler's credit with B019. I find that persuasive, so I now hold to two names. The chair's observation that B011 has exactly six explicit preferences is not evidence of merit. It is also a narrow lead that includes the chair and a frequent co-author of the secretary. I therefore tried to re-argue the case against B005, and I do not think the exchange has displaced B011. Neither of the two strongest objections to B011 (identification and the 2022 overlap) is a defect in the discovery. The first is a limit on what the evidence shows, and the second is a question of citation wording.
statement.case_against: The reservations are real. First, the collateral channel is better established as a mechanism and a reusable modelling component than as a measured magnitude. A prize citation should therefore credit the mechanism and not claim a quantified effect. Second, the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises is adjacent territory, and a committee could reasonably decide that macro-finance has been honoured recently. Third, a two-name award leaves out the quantitative financial-accelerator and policy-model strand (Gertler, Gilchrist), which carried these ideas into practice. That omission must be defended explicitly, not left implicit. Fourth, B005 is better tested against micro data. A committee that weights direct empirical confirmation heavily, as I often do in my own empirical work, could reasonably rank it above B011. I treat that as a legitimate difference in weighting and not as an error. The attribution questions around B005 (Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum; Krugman 2008; Helpman's separate entry) are the main thing that keeps me from ranking it first.

responses.point: Stromberg now proposes Kiyotaki and Moore only. He argues that the committee would have to defend which part of Gertler's work a citation covers, that the accelerator part overlaps with 2022, and that his strongest remaining work sits in the New Keynesian and intermediation literatures, which are separate ballot items.
responses.response: I agree, and I have moved with you. I proposed Gertler at the opening because his work on credit frictions in monetary-policy models is independent and substantial. Your point is that this work belongs to other achievements, not to the collateral-price feedback. That is the decisive consideration for me. A citation covering Gertler would have to name a different discovery, and that case should be argued on its own terms. I also agree with your caveat that the 2022 overlap is a reason to scrutinise the wording, not a reason to disqualify the mechanism. I would write the citation around collateral values, asset prices and dynamic amplification and avoid words such as banks, bank runs or financial intermediation.

responses.point: Krusell rejected adding Gertler. He said the accelerator works through borrower net worth and external finance premia, with different microfoundations, so it is a related mechanism and not a component of Kiyotaki-Moore, and that crediting Gertler here would muddy attribution across B011 and B019.
responses.response: This was the sharpest argument on the Gertler question, and it is what moved me from three names to two. I would add one point from my own side as a labour economist. The evidence for B011 is mostly indirect: the mechanism's repeated reuse and crisis-episode evidence, not clean micro identification. The committee should be honest about that in the citation. The wording should say the laureates showed how collateral constraints amplify shocks. It should not say they measured how large the effect is. I do not think this weakens the case for the prize, but it should shape the wording.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranked B011 sixth in the opening and says the 2022 overlap weighs more heavily than the B011 supporters allow. The B005 preference rests on the framework having been confronted with micro and register data, in contrast to a conceptually foundational but weakly identified credit-cycle model.
responses.response: I take the identification point seriously, and it is the objection that has stayed with me. My reading of the 2022 overlap differs. That citation concerned the role of banks and bank runs in crises. Kiyotaki-Moore concerns real-sector amplification when firms' borrowing is limited by collateral values, so I treat it as adjacent but distinct. On identification, I think a foundational mechanism can be recognised even when its quantitative size is not pinned down. The citation should then credit the mechanism and not any magnitude. I accept that this is a different kind of achievement from B005, and that a member who weights direct testing most heavily would reasonably rank them the other way. That is a weighting disagreement and not a factual one.

responses.point: Boppart prefers B005 but calls the choice with B011 closer than his opening ranks suggest. He agrees that Kiyotaki-Moore is a clean, well-confirmed two-author contribution and says he would not oppose B011 in a configuration with the same level of attribution care.
responses.response: I appreciate that, and I think the two of us are close on the substance. You asked what would resolve your concern. For me it is a narrow citation that says what is honoured (the collateral-price feedback loop) and what is not (the accelerator and bank-focused strands). If that is acceptable to you, your remaining objection is about the relative directness of the evidence, which I concede is a real advantage of B005. I have moved B005 into my alternatives for that reason. If B011 does not carry, I would support a Helpman-Melitz award with a citation anchored on firm heterogeneity and selection.

responses.point: Friberg prefers B005 for its direct confirmation on firm-level data. He concedes that Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum are an attribution problem and proposes anchoring the citation on the theoretical integration of firm heterogeneity into trade, not on the empirical discovery of exporter heterogeneity. He rejects widening to Redding.
responses.response: Your distinction between the theoretical integration and the empirical exporter facts is the clearest way I have seen to defend a two-name B005. It answers part of the attribution objection, although the Krugman 2008 overlap and Helpman's marginal credit independent of B020 still need to be stated explicitly. I agree that adding Redding would dilute the credit. This is why I now list B005 first among my alternatives. A draft citation I could support is: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, and for showing how reallocation across firms shapes the gains from trade. I still rank B011 first because its attribution line is shorter and its maturity is at least equal. I do not think the evidence separates the two by a wide margin.

responses.point: Dreber-Almenberg prefers B014 with Autor, Hanson and Katz. She rests the case on transparent designs that have been tested and replicated for a long time. She would keep Katz over Dorn because the skill-premium work anchors the labour-demand discovery, and she concedes that the task-based and trade-shock strands may be seen as two achievements.
responses.response: I agree that B014 has the strongest replication record among the labour candidates, and I keep it as an alternative. I still read the overlap with the 2023 and 2024 prizes as making the incremental credit harder to isolate than for B011 or B005. I also remain concerned that the task and trade-shock strands may be two achievements under a three-name cap. In response to the chair's question, I now place B005 ahead of B014 and B026 as my fallback. B005 is more mature and has been tested more directly. I drop B026 because its confirmation record is shorter and it relies on restricted administrative data.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises as covering enough adjacent ground to lower the priority of collateral-based amplification, or whether a narrow citation makes the distinction clear.

Whether excluding Gertler and Gilchrist gives a fair account of the financial-accelerator lineage. The strand is entangled with 2022 and with B019, but a two-name award has to say explicitly that it is not honouring it.

How much weight indirect empirical identification of the collateral channel should carry relative to the more direct firm-level testing of B005. I regard this as a genuine weighting disagreement and not a factual one.

If B005 becomes the working configuration: how to word a citation that does not overreach on the Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum contributions, and how much marginal credit Helpman has independent of Krugman 2008 and his separate B020 entry.

My assessments rely on general knowledge and the supplied committee text, and I have not independently verified any source. A single-part prize seems the workable assumption, because I have not found a pairing under the three-laureate cap that keeps B011's attribution clean.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. None of the credited names for B011, B005 or B014 appears among my listed frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler). My field of labour economics and the economics of crime is adjacent to B014, which I list as an alternative, and to B026, which I no longer list. That is field proximity and not a personal connection. I have no listed tie to Helpman, Melitz or Redding. Having presented the 2023 prize, I am not aware of any bearing on the present candidates. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
